p: News · Orsund opens a 4,200-pallet GDP cold hub in Rotterdam
Control tower open 24/7  ·  Rotterdam · Nairobi · Valparaíso · Singapore
Forced-air pre-cooling takes a box of roses from 18 °C to 2 °C in ninety minutes. Here is what it buys you at the Aalsmeer clock.
Written by a planner or engineer at one of our hubs. Questions go straight to them through the control tower.
A rose cut at 07:00 in Naivasha is still breathing at 18 °C by the time it is packed. If it goes onto an aircraft that warm, it spends the first hours of the flight heating up the boxes around it.
Forced-air pre-cooling pulls cold air through the boxes until the stems are at 2 °C. It takes about ninety minutes and adds almost nothing to the cost of the lane.
Growers who pre-cool with us report two to three extra days of vase life, and that shows up in the price at the clock.

/insights/reading-a-reefer-log-without-a.description: Supply air, return air, pulp temperature: which line on the chart tells you whether your fruit is fine, and which one is noise.
h1: Reading a reefer log without a data scientist
h3: Why we pre-cool roses before they fly
Reading a reefer log without a data scientist

p: News · Orsund opens a 4,200-pallet GDP cold hub in Rotterdam
Control tower open 24/7  ·  Rotterdam · Nairobi · Valparaíso · Singapore
Supply air, return air, pulp temperature: which line on the chart tells you whether your fruit is fine, and which one is noise.
Written by a planner or engineer at one of our hubs. Questions go straight to them through the control tower.
A reefer log has more lines than most people need. Here is how to read the three that matter.
Supply air is what the unit blows in. Return air is what comes back after passing the cargo. Pulp temperature is what the fruit actually is. When return and pulp agree, you are fine.
A return air reading that climbs for more than two hours while supply stays flat usually means blocked airflow, often from pallets loaded against the doors.
